# Assignment 2: Hypothesis testing and rejection probabilities
### Bojan Endrovski

## 1. Test for one proportion

### Question 1
```{r}
prop.test(x=13, n=20, p=0.5, alternative="two.sided")
```
For the sample size of 20 we get a p-value of 0.2636 (> 0.05) thus failing to reject the null hypothesis. We don't have enough evidence to claim that choosing the green door is significantly different from 50%.

### Question 2
```{r}
prop.test(x=130, n=200, p=0.5, alternative="two.sided")
```
For the sample size of 200 we get a p-value of 0.0000302 (< 0.05) thus rejecting the null hypothesis. We now have sufficient evidence to claim that choosing the green door is significantly different from 50%. The proportion is the same (65% of participants chose the green door), but the bigger sample size give us more statistical power.

### Question 3
### a)
```{r}
n <- 20
prob <- 0.6
smp <- rbinom(n, size=1, prob=prob)
prop.test(sum(smp), n=n, p=0.5, alternative="two.sided")
```
Running the experiment mutiple times we get widely different results. The sample estimates the probability anywhere from 0.3 to 0.7 and very high p-value.

### b)
```{r}
n <- 200
prob <- 0.6
smp <- rbinom(n, size=1, prob=prob)
prop.test(sum(smp), n=n, p=0.5, alternative="two.sided")
```
In comparison with a), the estimates of the probability is a lot closer to 0.6 but the p-value is under 0.05 on majority of the runs, rejecting the null hypotesis. The closer the probability estimate is to the true value of 0.6, the smaller the p-value.


### c)
```{r}
n <- 200
prob <- 0.5
smp <- rbinom(n, size=1, prob=prob)
prop.test(sum(smp), n=n, p=0.5, alternative="two.sided")
```
The p-value is high on most runs, not rejecting the null hypothesis even when the probability estimate is very close to 0.5


### d)
```{r}
n <- 20
prob <- 0.1
smp <- rbinom(n, size=1, prob=prob)
prop.test(sum(smp), n=n, p=0.5, alternative="two.sided")
```
Even with a small sample size we reject the null hypothesis on most runs, unless the probability is estimated at avery different value than 0.1 (ex. prob=0.35 p-value=0.2636)


### Question 4
```{r}
N <- 500
n <- 20
prob <- 0.6
rej <- rep(0, 500)
for (i in 1:N) {
  smp <- rbinom(n, size=1, prob=prob)
  res <- prop.test(sum(smp), n=n, p=0.5, alternative="two.sided")
  rej[i] <- res$p.value < 0.05
}
sprintf("a) Rejections: %d out of %d (probability: %.4f)", sum(rej), N, mean(rej))

n <- 200
prob <- 0.6
rej <- rep(0, 500)
for (i in 1:N) {
  smp <- rbinom(n, size=1, prob=prob)
  res <- prop.test(sum(smp), n=n, p=0.5, alternative="two.sided")
  rej[i] <- res$p.value < 0.05
}
sprintf("b) Rejections: %d out of %d (probability: %.4f)", sum(rej), N, mean(rej))

n <- 200
prob <- 0.5
rej <- rep(0, 500)
for (i in 1:N) {
  smp <- rbinom(n, size=1, prob=prob)
  res <- prop.test(sum(smp), n=n, p=0.5, alternative="two.sided")
  rej[i] <- res$p.value < 0.05
}
sprintf("c) Rejections: %d out of %d (probability: %.4f)", sum(rej), N, mean(rej))

n <- 20
prob <- 0.1
rej <- rep(0, 500)
for (i in 1:N) {
  smp <- rbinom(n, size=1, prob=prob)
  res <- prop.test(sum(smp), n=n, p=0.5, alternative="two.sided")
  rej[i] <- res$p.value < 0.05
}
sprintf("d) Rejections: %d out of %d (probability: %.4f)", sum(rej), N, mean(rej))
```
a) The probability of rejection is low due to the small sample
b) The probability of rejection is is much higher because of the bigger sample
c) The probability of rejection is low because the null hypothesis is indeed true
d) The probability of rejection is high, in-spite of the small sample due to the strong statistical effect

## 2. Test for two proportions

### Question 1
```{r}
xs <- c(18, 28)
ns <- c(30, 40)
prop.test(x=xs, n=ns, alternative="two.sided")
```
From this experiment we can't reject the null hypothesis that px == py. The is no sufficient evidence that the social interaction influences door choice.

### Question 2
```{r}
sz1 <-30
sz2 <- 40
smp1 <- rbinom(sz1, 1, 0.6)
smp2 <- rbinom(sz2, 1, 0.8)
xs <- c(sum(smp1), sum(smp2))
ns <- c(sz1, sz2)
prop.test(x=xs, n=ns, alternative="two.sided")
```
The null hypothesis is not rejected on more often that it is rejected, but with the sample sizes of 30 and 40 is hard to derive a conclusive answer. When the probability estimates are further apart, the p-value is smaller.
